implementation_notes: Python's locks and condition variables are separate objects rather than properties of every object - the threading documentation points out this difference from Java explicitly - so a monitor is a class holding a threading.Lock or RLock plus one threading.Condition per wait reason, with synchronized methods written as ordinary methods that take the lock via with. Condition.wait/notify require the lock to be held, wait releases it atomically, and Condition.wait_for(predicate) packages the mandatory predicate loop; queue.Queue is the standard-library monitor for producer/consumer handoff and is usually the better choice for that use case. On free-threaded builds (PEP 703) the GIL no longer hides coarse races, so the monitor has to be correct on its own merits.
pitfalls: Condition.wait/notify raise RuntimeError when the associated lock is not held, and wait may return spuriously: always re-test the predicate (wait_for does it for you).
The GIL is not a monitor: it does not make multi-statement invariants atomic, and free-threaded builds remove even the accidental protection of single bytecodes.
Blocking a threading lock inside asyncio code stalls the event loop; asyncio primitives are not thread-safe, so mixing the two worlds needs run_in_executor or an explicit handoff.

variants.name: asyncio.Lock / asyncio.Condition (task-level)
variants.implementation_notes: For asyncio tasks the threading primitives would block the event loop, so the monitor is rebuilt from asyncio.Lock and asyncio.Condition: a Condition combines a lock with an Event-like wait, and its wait releases the lock while the task is suspended, which is the exact analogue of a monitor condition. Neither primitive is thread-safe, they must be created in the running loop, acquires are fair (FIFO) for asyncio.Lock, and timeouts come from asyncio.wait_for rather than a timeout argument. The same predicate-loop discipline applies because Condition.wait may return spuriously, and the same interface/implementation split prevents nested acquisitions of the non-reentrant lock.
variants.code_sketch:
async def put(self, item) -> None:
    async with self._cond:                       # await acquire/release
        await self._cond.wait_for(lambda: len(self._q) < self._cap)
        self._q.append(item)
        self._cond.notify_all()
pitfalls: asyncio primitives are bound to the running loop and are not thread-safe: creating them at import time or using them from a thread pool fails, and a threading.Condition in the same path blocks the loop entirely.

Only awaits are suspension points: a long CPU-bound block inside the critical section still blocks the loop, and awaiting inside the section lets other tasks observe the state before it is consistent unless the invariant is re-established before releasing.
notify() raises RuntimeError when the lock is not held and wakes only one waiter when several predicates share the condition: prefer notify_all.
